ImageDescription.value: Humoristic cartoon from Puck on the establishment of diplomatic relations between Greece and Persia. In 499 BC, the Persian Achaemenid Empire tried unsuccessfully to conquer various ancient Greek city-states. Finally in 449 BC a de facto peace was concluded and the Greco-Persian Wars effectively ended. In 1902, Mozaffar ad-Din Shah of Persia and George I of Greece agreed to de jure recognition and after 2393 years established diplomatic relations. This of course ignores a long history of Greco-Persian interactions thereafter throughout Antiquity, not least the Peace of Antalcidas, the conquests of Alexander the Great and the Seleucid Empire, or even the long history of the Byzantine-Persian wars.

Credit.value: Puck, 31 December 1902, Library of Congress

ImageDescription.value: Bas-relief of Ramesses II on his chariot during the Battle of Kadesh against the Hittite Empire under Muwatalli II, south wall in the Hypostyle Hall of the Great Temple of Abu Simbel, Egypt. The Great Temple at Abu Simbel, which took about twenty years to build, was completed around year 24 of the reign of Ramesses the Great (which corresponds to 1265 BC). It was dedicated to the gods Amun, Ra-Horakhty, and Ptah, as well as to the deified Ramesses himself. It is generally considered the grandest and most beautiful of the temples commissioned during the reign of Ramesses II, and one of the most beautiful in Egypt.

ImageDescription.value:
Jewish cemetery in Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
In Dülmen, the old Jewish cemetery was located at Lüdinghausen Gate – a burial site that had been used by Jewish community members since the early 17th century and existed until 1937. The dead of the Jewish community were buried there before a new cemetery was later established on Kapellenweg.
In 1937, under pressure from the National Socialists and against the will of the Jewish community, the old cemetery was closed and the land sold. The gravestones of those buried there were moved to the then newer Jewish cemetery on Kapellenweg, but no exhumations took place within the tight deadline.
After the cemetery was leveled, the vacated area was given the name Hindenburgplatz, named after the former Reich President Paul von Hindenburg. This square was created directly on the site of the former burial ground. Parts of the graves that had not yet been removed were covered; the local NSDAP used a swastika flower bed to plant the square, which symbolically represented the desecration of a sacred place.
After the end of World War II, the name Hindenburgplatz was no longer officially used. The former cemetery area was later built over or used as green space, and it was not until decades later that people began to remember its former use and the Jewish community.
Today, a memorial at the site of the old cemetery, the former Jewish cemetery outside the Lüdinghausen Gate gate, commemorates the Jewish citizens of Dülmen and their history.

ImageDescription.value:
Cranes at the Elbphilharmonie (southeast corner) in Hamburg, Germany
The Elbphilharmonie Hamburg is one of Hamburg’s most famous landmarks. It is located in HafenCity on the former Kaispeicher A, a brick warehouse dating from 1963. A spectacular glass building with a wave-shaped roof was constructed on top of this historic foundation.
The design is by Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron. Construction began in 2007, and after delays and considerable cost increases, the building opened in January 2017. The total cost was significantly higher than originally planned, which sparked nationwide debate.
The centerpiece is the Grand Hall with around 2,100 seats and exceptional acoustics, developed by acoustician Yasuhisa Toyota. In addition to concert halls, the Elbphilharmonie houses a hotel, apartments, and a publicly accessible plaza with panoramic views of the harbour and city. It is considered a cultural symbol of Hamburg and one of the most modern concert halls in the world.

ImageDescription.value:
Observation window in the wall of the walkways at the Dülmen-Visbeck Special Ammunition Storage, Dernekamp, Kirchspiel, Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Bundeswehr Ammunition Depot, located approximately 4.5 km south of Dülmen, was built between 1963 and 1965 as part of the St. Barbara Barracks in Dülmen. The special ammunition storage (SAS) within the ammunition depot was put into operation by the US Army in 1969. Over time, and particularly in the 1980s, the special ammunition storage in particular was made significantly more secure. The special ammunition storage was abandoned in the early 1990s, as was the ammunition depot in 1996. It passed into private hands. The town of Dülmen acquired the site in 2017 and it has been open to visitors on guided tours since 2019.

ImageDescription.value:
Position light (with image of St. Christopher) of a Rolls-Royce Phantom II in Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Rolls-Royce Phantom II was built by Rolls-Royce from 1929 to 1936 and was a further development of the Phantom I. It was considered the epitome of luxurious automotive engineering in the interwar period.
Technically, the Phantom II had a 7.7-liter inline six-cylinder engine that was known for its smooth running and reliability. The chassis was improved, among other things, with a new frame construction and optimized suspension, which increased driving comfort and road holding.
As was customary at the time, Rolls-Royce mainly supplied the chassis; the bodies were individually built by renowned coachbuilders such as Park Ward or Mulliner. This resulted in elegant limousines, Pullman models, and sporty variants such as the Continental.
The Phantom II quickly became a status symbol for royalty, industrialists, and movie stars. It is one of the most sought-after pre-war classic cars and stands for technical perfection, quality craftsmanship, and timeless elegance.

ImageDescription.value:
Hood ornament “Spirit of Ecstasy” (commonly known as “Emily”) of a Rolls-Royce Phantom II in Dülmen, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
The Rolls-Royce Phantom II was built by Rolls-Royce from 1929 to 1936 and was a further development of the Phantom I. It was considered the epitome of luxurious automotive engineering in the interwar period.
Technically, the Phantom II had a 7.7-liter inline six-cylinder engine that was known for its smooth running and reliability. The chassis was improved, among other things, with a new frame construction and optimized suspension, which increased driving comfort and road holding.
As was customary at the time, Rolls-Royce mainly supplied the chassis; the bodies were individually built by renowned coachbuilders such as Park Ward or Mulliner. This resulted in elegant limousines, Pullman models, and sporty variants such as the Continental.
The Phantom II quickly became a status symbol for royalty, industrialists, and movie stars. It is one of the most sought-after pre-war classic cars and stands for technical perfection, quality craftsmanship, and timeless elegance.
